# Results — Study 264 (Buffett-Indicator) on the S&P 500 price tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The Buffett Indicator
(total US market cap / GDP, year-end, in percent of GDP) is hardcoded in
[`data.py`](../buffett_indicator/data.py) (1971–2025, 55 readings). Forward
returns are S&P 500 (`^GSPC`) **price** calendar-year returns from the repo-level
split-only cache (`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`). Match the fingerprint below
to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC split-only price index (Dec/Dec calendar-year return) | fwd years 1972–2026 | 55 | `479252b8a735` |
| Buffett Indicator (market cap / GDP, year-end) | 1971–2025 | 55 readings | hardcoded constant |

The indicator at year-end **Y** is matched to the S&P 500 price return earned in
year **Y+1** — one full year of execution lag, no look-ahead.

## Primary spec — predictive regression (next-year return on valuation level)

`fwd_ret_{Y+1} = α + β · ratio_Y + ε`, OLS with a Newey-West (HAC) t-stat.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Slope β (per +100pp of GDP) | **−3.22 pp** of next-year return |
| Pearson correlation | **−0.093** |
| R² | **0.009** |
| HAC t-stat on β | **−0.92** |
| n | 55 |

The slope has the **sign Buffett predicts** (more expensive → lower forward
return), but it is statistically indistinguishable from zero: |t| = 0.92, far
below the |t| ≥ 2 bar. The indicator explains under **1%** of the variance of
next-year returns.

## Terciles — cheap vs expensive years (in-sample breakpoints)

| Bucket | n | mean next-yr return | up-rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Cheap (lowest third) | 19 | **+10.0%** | 78.9% |
| Mid | 22 | +9.9% | 77.3% |
| Expensive (highest third) | 14 | **+8.2%** | 64.3% |

Expensive years do under-return cheap years by ~1.8 pp/yr in the predicted
direction — but these are *in-sample* tercile breakpoints (look-ahead: you could
not know in 1995 that 96% would be a "mid" reading). And +8.2%/yr after an
"expensive" reading is still a perfectly good return — hardly a reason to "leave
the party."

## Sub-periods

| Window | corr(ratio, fwd_ret) | note |
|---|--:|---|
| 1971–1994 (pre-bubble) | mildly negative | indicator rarely above 100% |
| 1995–2025 (modern) | mildly negative | indicator above 100% for most years yet the market kept compounding |

The relationship is the same weak negative sign in both halves; nothing
strengthens it. The modern era is the killer for *tradability*: the indicator
crossed 100% in 1996 and, apart from 2002 and 2008–09, essentially never looked
"cheap" again — yet the S&P compounded at ~8%/yr price-only.

## Could you trade it? — the real-time timing strategy

Long the S&P only when the indicator is at or below its **expanding** (point-in-
time) median, else sit in cash (price-only, cash earns 0%). The expanding median
is the honest "is it expensive?" test — no hindsight thresholds.

| Strategy | CAGR (gross) | CAGR (net, 10 bps/flip) | years invested | regime flips |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Buffett timing (long-when-cheap) | **+1.31%** | +1.30% | **23.6%** | 4 |
| Buy-and-hold S&P (price) | **+8.11%** | — | 100% | 0 |

The timing rule sits in cash **76% of the years** — almost the entire post-1995
bull market — and earns **1.3%/yr** against buy-and-hold's **8.1%/yr**. The
excess return (strat − buy-and-hold) has a HAC t-stat of **−3.76**: the strategy
*reliably destroys* return. Turnover is trivial (4 flips in 55 years, costs a
rounding error) — the problem is not costs, it is that the rule keeps you out of
the market for a generation.

## Positive control

On the synthetic tape, a planted mean-reversion slope is recovered cleanly:
β = −0.05 gives a regression t of **−3.7** (n=400); β = −0.15 gives **−10.1**;
the null (β = 0) gives **−0.5**. The engine finds a valuation→return link when
one exists. The real tape's |t| = 0.92 is a statement about the **market and
sample size**, not the method.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The slope has the right (negative) sign and is backed by a
  large valuation-predictability literature, but on the real tape the HAC t-stat
  is only **−0.92** (R² < 1%). It clears neither the |t| ≥ 2 bar for `REAL` nor
  the higher hurdle the literature now demands for valuation ratios. The
  forward-return tape is **price-only** (survivorship is a non-issue here — it is
  the index — but the no-dividends caveat is named on this axis).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** A real-time "leave the party when expensive" rule
  earns **1.3%/yr** versus **8.1%/yr** buy-and-hold (excess t = −3.76), because
  market-cap/GDP has been above its own history for almost thirty years while the
  market compounded anyway. The Buffett Indicator is a thermometer, not a timer:
  it tells you the temperature of the room, not when to leave the party.
